title: The Assumption (15 August)
hookLine: Mary taken up; in many places a public holiday with processions
last: IT IS GOOD TO BE HERE.

cards: On the fifteenth of August, much of southern Europe shuts down. In Italy it's Ferragosto, and the cities empty out for the beach.

But in a village square in Sicily, or a coastal town in Portugal, a statue of Mary leaves the church on the shoulders of men in white shirts, under strings of lights, with a band playing and fireworks after dark.
In Poland, people bring bunches of herbs and flowers to be blessed. It's high summer, and the feast is about the end of a life.

teach.b: Catholics believe that at the end of her earthly life, Mary was taken up, body and soul, into heavenly glory. Assumption is from the Latin assumere, to take up.
Notice the verb: Jesus ascends, by his own power; Mary is assumed, taken up by God. The belief is very old.
In the Christian East, the feast is called the Dormition, the falling asleep of Mary, kept on this same date. Stories circulated early about the apostles gathered at her deathbed, and an empty tomb.
But the Bible says nothing about how Mary's life ended, and the Church doesn't pretend it does.
Only in 1950 did Pope Pius XII formally define the Assumption as dogma, and he chose his words carefully: having completed the course of her earthly life. He did not say whether she died first.
The Orthodox speak of her falling asleep; some Catholic theologians hold that she died; the definition leaves the question open.

teach.h: A WOMAN CLOTHED WITH THE SUN.
teach.b: On the feast, the Church reads from Revelation, in the Douay-Rheims: "a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars." Why does it matter?
Catholics read it as a promise about everyone: not just a soul surviving, but the whole person, body included, raised. She went first.
And week ninety-seven closes: the Sacred Heart, John's birth, Peter and Paul, Mary Magdalene, Joachim and Anne, the Transfiguration, and now the Assumption.

how: The Assumption on 15 August is a solemnity and, in many countries, a holy day of obligation; in much of Europe and Latin America it's a public holiday with processions carrying a statue of Mary, and in Poland and elsewhere herbs and flowers are blessed.

games.q: you're Pius XII in 1950, defining the Assumption. theologians disagree about whether Mary died first. what do you write?
o: that she died, and was then taken up.
having completed the course of her earthly life, leaving it open.
games.why: he chose words that settle the Assumption and leave the question of her death open.

practice: Walk slowly, at a procession's pace, the way a village procession sets off at dusk: outside as the day cools if you can, through your home if you can't, or along an evening road in your mind. Think of someone you love who has died.
If you pray, pray a Hail Mary as you walk, or pray for them; if you don't, carry their memory along with you.

wordCard.voice: The Assumption. Mary taken up, body and soul, into heavenly glory at the end of her earthly life. Defined in 1950; kept on the fifteenth of August. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: a taking up, from assumere — Mary is taken up, not ascending by her own power.

carryVoice: Your line: she went ahead. Where she went, Christians hope to follow. See you tomorrow.
